title: Variables & Data Types
description: Learn how to store, select, convert, validate, and display data in C#. Complete every five-question quiz to unlock the next lesson and prepare for operators and expressions.
completionText: You are ready for Module 3, where stored values become useful expressions through arithmetic, comparison, logical, and assignment operators.

lessons.title: Introduction to Variables
objectives: Explain a variable as a named location used to store a value.
Declare variables using a C# type and meaningful name.
Assign initial values and update values later.
theory: A program becomes useful when it can remember information. A game may remember a player's name, score, health, or level. C# commonly stores these values in variables.
A variable is a named storage location. Instead of repeatedly writing 100, a program can store it as playerHealth. The name communicates meaning and allows later access or change.
C# is strongly typed. int score; declares a whole-number variable. score = 250; assigns a value. int score = 250; combines both steps.
Assignment stores the right-hand value in the left-hand variable. Therefore score = score + 50; reads the score, adds 50, and stores the new result.
Use descriptive camelCase names such as studentAge. Names cannot contain spaces, begin with digits, or use reserved C# keywords.
terms: A named location that stores a value.
Specifying a variable's type and name.
Storing a value with the equals sign.
lessons.tryIt: Create variables for your name, course, year of study, and whether you enjoy programming. Print and update them.
lessons.challenge: Create a character profile containing name, level, health, movement speed, and alive status.
mistakes: Use double quotation marks around strings.
End declarations with semicolons.
Do not begin names with numbers.
Remember that score and Score differ.
lessons.summary: Variables give meaningful names to stored values. Declaration supplies type and name; assignment stores or replaces a value.
quiz: A variable is a named storage location.
int score; declares a whole-number variable.
studentAge is descriptive and valid camelCase.
Reassignment replaces the previous value with 4.

lessons.title: Primitive Data Types
objectives: Describe int, double, float, decimal, char, bool, and string.
theory: A data type defines what a variable stores and which operations are valid. int stores signed whole numbers and commonly uses four bytes.
double uses eight bytes for general fractional calculations. float uses four bytes and requires an f suffix. Float is common in graphics and Unity APIs.
decimal uses sixteen bytes and high base-10 precision, making it suitable for money. Decimal literals use an m suffix.
char stores one character in single quotes. bool stores true or false. string stores text in double quotes.
Choose according to meaning, range, and precision. Float and double represent many decimal values approximately.
lessons.tryIt: Choose suitable types for age, average mark, balance, middle initial, enrolment status, and full name.
lessons.challenge: Build a product record using at least six different types and print every value.
mistakes: Use single quotes for char and double quotes for string.
Add f to float and m to decimal literals.
Do not store fractions in int.
Prefer decimal for financial calculations.
lessons.summary: Types define valid values, memory, precision, and operations. Choose types according to the data's meaning.
quiz: Best type for number of lives?
A char uses single quotation marks.
The f suffix marks a float literal.
Type for whether a door is open?

lessons.title: Declaring and Initialising Variables
theory: A declaration introduces a variable's type and name. Assignment stores a value. Initialisation gives a variable its first value, often in the declaration.
Combining declaration and initialisation is clear because the starting state is immediately visible. Separate them when the value is only known after another operation.
Fields receive automatic defaults, but local variables must be definitely assigned before they can be read.
The default keyword requests a type's default value: int becomes 0 and bool becomes false.
Use descriptive camelCase names. Avoid unexplained abbreviations and do not include the type in the name.
terms: The first value assigned to a variable.
A variable declared inside a method or block.
A variable declared as part of a type.
A naming style such as favouriteColour.
lessons.tryIt: Declare one variable separately, then create three variables using combined declaration and initialisation.
lessons.challenge: Write eight clearly named variables: four with separate assignment and four with combined initialisation.
mistakes: Assign local variables before reading them.
End declarations with semicolons.
Do not use spaces or leading digits in names.
Keep capitalisation consistent.
lessons.summary: Declaration introduces type and name, assignment stores a value, and initialisation supplies the first value.
quiz: int total; introduces the type and name only.
The declaration includes the first value.
Can an unassigned local int be printed?
Local variables must be definitely assigned.
The default Boolean value is false.

lessons.title: Constants
theory: A regular variable can change. A constant represents a value that must remain fixed throughout the program.
A constant uses const, a type, a name, and a value. It must be initialised in its declaration and cannot later be reassigned.
Constants suit compile-time values such as conversion factors, fixed limits, and repeated labels.
Named constants replace unexplained magic numbers. SecondsPerMinute communicates more meaning than a repeated literal 60.
Use const only for genuinely fixed values, not player health, user input, or runtime calculations.
terms: A named value that cannot be reassigned.
The C# keyword used for constants.
A naming style often used for constants.
lessons.tryIt: Create constants for DaysPerWeek, PassingMark, and CollegeName, then regular variables for changing values.
lessons.challenge: Build a ticket calculator with fixed TicketPrice and MaximumTickets.
mistakes: Initialise every constant immediately.
Do not use const for user input.
Never reassign a constant.
Use a compatible type and suffix.
lessons.summary: Constants protect genuinely fixed values and replace unexplained literals with meaningful names.
quiz: A const requires an initial value.
What if a constant is reassigned?
Named constants explain repeated fixed values.

lessons.title: Type Conversion
theory: Type conversion creates a value of one type from another. An implicit conversion occurs automatically when C# considers it safe.
An int can be assigned to double implicitly. A potentially lossy conversion such as double to int requires an explicit cast.
(int)9.8 produces 9 by removing the fractional portion; it does not round.
Convert methods such as Convert.ToInt32 provide readable conversions and may use different rounding behaviour.
Always consider destination range and precision. Double-to-float conversion may lose significant digits.
lessons.tryIt: Convert an int to double, cast 27.89 to int, and compare it with Convert.ToInt32.
lessons.challenge: Display cast, Convert.ToInt32, and float versions of a temperature.
mistakes: A cast to int truncates.
Invalid text can cause conversion exceptions.
Check range before narrowing.
Do not assume precision is preserved.
lessons.summary: Widening conversions may be implicit. Potentially lossy conversions require casts or conversion methods.
quiz: A cast places the destination type in parentheses.

lessons.title: Reading User Input
objectives: Write clear prompts and validation messages.
theory: Console.ReadLine() waits for input and returns the entered line as a string, even when the user types digits.
Use Console.Write before reading input so the response appears beside the prompt. A null-coalescing fallback can provide an empty string.
Parse methods convert correctly formatted strings but throw exceptions for invalid text.
TryParse returns true on success and places the converted result in an out variable. Invalid text produces false rather than an ordinary format exception.
Boolean parsing recognises true or false. Numeric parsing may depend on regional number formatting.
terms: A method that reads a line as text.
A conversion that throws for invalid format.
A safe conversion reporting success or failure.
The variable receiving a converted result.
lessons.tryIt: Ask for name, age, average mark, and submission status. Use TryParse for non-text values.
lessons.challenge: Create a game survey with safely validated hours, rating, and recommendation status.
mistakes: ReadLine returns text.
Parse can fail on invalid format.
Check TryParse's Boolean result.
State the expected input format.
lessons.summary: ReadLine collects text. Convert it when another type is needed, and use TryParse for uncertain input.
quiz: TryParse reports success without ordinary format exceptions.
The out variable receives the converted value.
Boolean parsing recognises true and false.
Why use Console.Write for a prompt?
Write does not add a line break.

lessons.title: String Interpolation and Concatenation
theory: Concatenation joins values using the plus operator. When one operand is a string, compatible values are converted to text.
String interpolation begins with a dollar sign and places values or expressions inside braces.
Interpolation usually remains clearer when messages contain several values.
Formatting such as F2 displays two decimal places, while currency formatting uses the current culture.
Be careful with numeric plus operations. "Total: " + 2 + 3 produces Total: 23; parentheses or interpolation can produce 5.
terms: Joining values into a string with +.
lessons.tryIt: Print a student result once with concatenation and once with interpolation.
lessons.challenge: Create an item receipt with quantity, unit price, total, and two decimal places.
mistakes: Place $ before the opening quote.
Use braces around interpolated expressions.
Include spaces in concatenated fragments.
Use parentheses around numeric addition.
lessons.summary: Concatenation joins values with +. Interpolation places expressions inside braces and is often clearer.
quiz: String concatenation proceeds left to right.
F2 formats a number with two decimal places.

lessons.title: Practice Project · User Information Program
objectives: Collect name, age, favourite game, and colour.
theory: This project combines the Module 2 workflow. It asks for a name, age, favourite game, and favourite colour.
Name, game, and colour use string. Age uses int after validation.
Use Console.Write for clear prompts and ReadLine with an empty-string fallback for text.
Use int.TryParse for age. If conversion fails, display a helpful message instead of producing the profile.
When input is valid, display labelled values and an expression for age next year.
terms: A structured collection of related values.
lessons.tryIt: Type the project, test valid and invalid ages, and add one more well-named field.
lessons.challenge: Add weekly gaming hours and recommendation status. Validate both before displaying all fields.
mistakes: Do not treat ReadLine as an int before conversion.
Use age only after successful TryParse.
Check every quote, brace, and semicolon.
Keep prompts and output labels consistent.
lessons.summary: You can declare variables, choose types, define constants, convert values, validate input, and build readable output.
quiz: A name is a sequence of characters.
TryParse safely reports whether conversion succeeds.
Module 3 applies operators to stored values.
